name: regexrare
algorithm: Find of two patterns whose literal prefix is rare in the text ("#[0-9]+", one byte; "needle[0-9]+", six bytes), each planted once near the end of mib MiB of log-like text from splitmix64(seed), byte for byte the same in every language, reps times (README.md); variant gen runs them as Mk gen regex.Matcher code, and Go, which has no build-time regex, runs its compiled regexps there too; variants eng and enggen draw the letters by English frequency and look for theseus[0-9]+ and needle[0-9]+ (SV-10).

skip.c: no std regex in C (POSIX regex.h is not ISO C, and the MSVC CRT has none)
skip.rust: no std regex in Rust (the regex crate is not std; no crate stands in)
skip.mk-wrap: the checksum already uses the wrapping operators

variants.name: gen
notes: The same patterns as gen regex.Matcher code: its emitted prefilter RxPre. Go's cell is regexp.MustCompile as in variant compile.

variants.name: eng
notes: Review finding SV-10: the text's letters in English frequency proportions, and the patterns theseus[0-9]+ and needle[0-9]+, whose first and last bytes are common there (t and s, n and e) while their rarest pair is not (h and u, d and l).

variants.name: enggen
notes: Variant eng as gen regex.Matcher code (RxPre). Go's cell is regexp.MustCompile as in variant eng.

no_counts: B24 does not apply: an idiomatic row compares libraries, each with its own algorithm; the checksum (the match starts) checks that every engine found the same matches
notes: The text: each byte from splitmix64, 26 in 32 a lowercase letter, 3 a space, 2 a digit, 1 a newline; 'needle42 #7 ' written 100 bytes before the end. '#' never occurs elsewhere, so the one-byte prefilter is a memchr over the whole text; 'n' and 'e' are frequent, so the pair filter keeps about one position in 1,024 and verifies it.
Idiomatic standard library (plan/06-m6.md 4.1): Mk regex.Compile and Regex.Find on a str; Go regexp.MustCompile and FindIndex on a []byte. Every language builds the text inside its timed run.
